The cylinder never moves at all. You spend the next while working the maintenance cover back onto its lugs one-handed, because leaving a Citadel seal hanging open behind you is not something you are willing to do.

outcomes.success:
You stop reading the symbols in the order they appear and start grouping them against the relay interval instead. The display is not changing the code. It is showing you one code against a clock, and once you have the grouping the shifting stops meaning anything.

You run the sequence twice more before you trust it, and twice the display agrees with you. Then you say it aloud, and again fifty paces east, and again at the junction after that, until it belongs to you rather than to the door.
outcomes.failure:
One symbol in six turns over on every third relay click, and you build a pattern around it three separate times before accepting that the pattern is being built around you. Which version does the Citadel expect? The display has no opinion on the matter.

You leave with nothing in your head that will survive the walk east, and with the particular taste of a puzzle almost had. Behind you the six symbols cycle and go black and start again, which they would do whether or not anyone had ever stood here.

events.body:
The East Citadel comes up out of the haze in straight vertical lines, the first straight lines the road has shown you since the Outskirts. Floodlights strike together and pin you flat against the outer blast door, and through your boots the concrete carries the vibration of machinery that has never once been allowed to stop. Above the door, rifle apertures open in sequence. You count six.

A loudspeaker asks for the current challenge response. It is a recorded woman's voice, level and unhurried, the kind that once read platform numbers to people holding luggage. Beside the door a panel wakes: a reader collar, six empty slots, and under them a countdown in red digits that does not speed up for anyone.

You have nothing that fits the collar or the slots. Nothing you carried up out of the tunnels answers a question shaped like that, and the digits are not waiting for you to think of something.

What you do have is on you. Salt in the seams of your coat, marsh water dried gray to the knee, soot ground into the cuffs, glass dust in the welt of each boot, brake dust laid over all of it like a signature. That is a record a person could read, if a person is anywhere behind the speaker.

The digits pass the halfway mark. Make somebody up there decide you are worth interrupting the machine for, or stand here and learn what the countdown counts toward.

outcomes.success:
You give the panel what the door below gave you, and the panel takes it. The six slots fill one at a time and hold. For two seconds nothing else happens. Then the countdown stops with digits still on it, and the outer door begins withdrawing its locks, one layer, then the next, each a different note in the concrete.

The rifle apertures do not close. You cross the threshold under six barrels that track you the whole way, and the recorded voice says PROCEED TO SCREENING as if you had arrived on the right day at the right hour.

Beyond the outer door is a walled court with cold lamps in the ceiling and a floor cleaner than any surface you have touched since the Outskirts. Salt and glass dust fall off your coat onto it and lie there, obvious. At the far end an inner gate stands shut, and behind it something heavy is moving on tracks, unhurried, coming to look at you closer. The door seals at your back, and the sound of the road outside stops as if it had never been there.
outcomes.failure:
You give the panel what the door below gave you, and five of the six slots take it. The sixth flickers and rejects: one symbol belongs to an older cycle, shuffled out by relays clicking somewhere east while you were still walking. You are reaching to correct it when the first aperture fires.

It is warning fire, aimed at the concrete a hand's width from your boot, but the concrete comes apart and the fragments do not know the difference. Something goes through your calf and something else opens your forearm to the elbow, and you are down on one knee against the door with the digits still running over your head.

The countdown reaches zero. Nothing happens for one held breath, and then the locks withdraw anyway, layer by layer, and the door swings inward on a lit court with a floor you leave a trail across. The Citadel is not admitting you. It has decided to look at you closer, on its own side of the door, where the guns can see better. At the far end of the court an inner gate stands shut, and beyond it something heavy has started to move.
outcomes.critical_success:
You give the panel what the door below gave you and add the thing the door could not: the timing, the pause the eastern relays leave after the fourth group when their load is steady. All six slots fill together. The countdown does not stop; it clears, and the digits are replaced by a single line you were not meant to be able to read: CIVIL DEFENSE TRAFFIC, EXPECTED.

The rifle apertures close, in the same order they opened. A narrow personnel door beside the blast door unbolts itself, and a strip of green lamps comes on along the corridor behind it, at ankle height, the way lamps are set to lead people who have been told to keep their heads down.

You go in walking, not driven. The corridor takes you past pipe runs and a row of numbered lockers into a lit screening court, and on the way your thinking comes clear and orderly for the first time in days, each problem sitting apart from the next where you can pick it up. It lasts. At the far end of the court an inner gate stands closed. Something on tracks is moving behind it, and it has not yet been told that you were expected.

outcomes.success:
You do not answer the question. You talk over it.

You give the speaker the blocks in the west with their tables still set and nobody at them. You give it the flats, and how far a radio carries across salt with nobody left to hear it. The black water in the marches. The yards where the pipes are still hot and nobody tends them. The ground east of the yards that sings underfoot and burns a shadow into any wall left standing. The tunnels under all of it, and how each stretch has been claimed by sound and by barrier. You give it distances in days and water in bottles, and you do not stop for breath, because the digits do not stop either.

At eleven the countdown pauses. A different voice comes through the speaker, a man's, live, with a cough in it, and says that execution is deferred pending screening. He does not say welcome. The outer door withdraws its locks and opens on a cold-lit court, and the rifles above follow you all the way across the threshold. At the far end an inner gate stands shut, and behind it something heavy moves on tracks, coming to do what the man on the speaker could not decide to do himself.
outcomes.failure:
You talk over the question, fast, with the blocks and the flats and the marsh water in it, and somewhere in the second sentence you hear your own voice do the thing it does when it is asking for its life. Whoever is behind the speaker hears it too. They have been trained to hear that and to call it contamination.

The recorded voice requests supporting evidence. You are still reaching for your pack when the stun round takes you in the chest.

The floodlights go white and then go away.

You come back on a concrete floor under cold ceiling lamps with your ribs on fire down the left side and blood in your mouth from where your teeth met. Your hands will not hold still. You are inside the outer door, in a lit court you did not walk into, with the road's dust smeared under you in the shape of a body being dragged. Someone decided you were more use examined than shot, and it was not kindness. At the far end of the court the inner gate is shut, and something heavy is moving behind it on tracks.

events.body:
The screening court is lit from above by cold lamps that leave nothing on the floor to hide behind. The inner gate opens far enough to let an armored Warden roll out on tracks somebody has kept maintained. Its wheel assembly is damaged on the near side and cuts a bright groove across the concrete as it comes.

Scanners travel over you, the wounds, the pack, the coat with six regions of dust in it, and the machine declares contamination beyond admission limits in a recorded woman's voice, the same one the loudspeaker used at the outer door. It says it twice. The rotary cannon on its turret has already begun to turn.

One sensor on the housing flickers each time the turret swings, a dead interval you could time. Behind the arc it patrols, a manual gate control stands on a pedestal with its cover open. This machine was built to outlast argument. Getting past it means blinding it, breaking it, or crossing the fraction of the court it cannot see.

outcomes.success: You wait for the flicker and put your signal into the sensor during its refresh, and the Warden's picture of the court fills with bodies that are not there. The turret swings toward the nearest ghost and fires at bare concrete, then at the next. Its voice keeps refusing entry to positions where nobody stands. You cross behind its arc while it is busy with them and put your hand on the manual control, and its attention never once comes back to you.
outcomes.failure: The sensor takes your interference, works on it, and traces it to the source before the overload settles: you. The turret comes around in one motion and the cannon's first burst goes across your side like a bar taken out of a fire, and the smell arrives with the pain. But the damaged sensor cannot confirm what it hit. The machine sweeps on to make sure of you and sweeps blind, and you drag yourself under that blind pass to the manual control with your coat still smoking.

outcomes.victory: The Warden fights like a law that never expected an appeal. You go for the wheel assembly, the damaged side, and go for it again every time the cannon has to cool, until the mount gives, the armor folds down over the track, and the turret comes off its ring and strikes the concrete face first. It does not stop talking. Contamination beyond admission limits, it says to the floor, in the same recorded voice. The inner controls wait beyond its body, and nothing on the court is aiming at you.

outcomes.success: You watch the tracking beam make three full sweeps and find the place where its return leaves a gap, one narrow absence about a stride and a half wide, there and gone. On the fourth pass you are in it, and then behind the turret before its calculations catch up. The cannon fires at the concrete you were standing on. Your hand is on the manual control while the machine is still searching an empty court for the thing that was just there.
outcomes.failure: The beam reverses early, before the damaged motor should be able to swing it, and you are in the open when it does. The burst catches you across the back and the legs and throws you the last stride. You get up because there is nowhere to lie down, and you cover the remaining ground in a stagger that costs more than the run did, with the sound of the turret already coming back around. Your hand reaches the manual control while the Warden is acquiring your position again, one weapon at a time.

events.body:
The inner gate opens no wider than a hand. Clean air comes through the gap, smelling of rain and filtered metal, and the drive that opened it is grinding somewhere inside the wall, a note that keeps dropping toward the pitch of a thing about to stop for good.

The gate leaves are as thick as a person is wide. A stenciled plate beside the seam says what happens when the drive fails: the leaves close under their own weight and lock, and the edges of the seam are scored to bright metal by something that did not get clear in time. The emergency controller is mounted below the plate, a small panel with a red-bordered diagram and a voltage rating with more digits than you have fingers; the last hand that tried it left a glove fused to the frame.

Behind you the Warden is not dead. Its cannon motor is turning over, slow, then less slow. One weapon at a time, it is coming back.

Above the seam a guard watches through armored glass. Above the guard, the rifle apertures from the outer door have their counterparts here, and one of them is open.

Nothing yet requires you to touch the seam, the panel, or the glass. The air keeps coming through the gap, and the count has nothing to do with you: the gate closes when the drive quits, the Warden fires when it can, and every mistake left ends within sight of shelter.

outcomes.success:
You put both hands into the seam and push. Nothing gives for the length of a breath, and then the drive inside the wall, already failing, fails a little further, and old gears surrender teeth one at a time with a sound like bone. The gap widens to a shoulder, then a body. Behind you the Warden's cannon finds its speed and fires, and the burst hits the closing edge of the leaf where your back was, and you are already through.

The gate seals on your final step. The lock engages with a sound you feel in your sternum, and the clean air is everywhere, and your lungs, which had stopped believing in it, take it in with a noise you did not authorize. On the far side of the glass, someone in a Citadel uniform is looking at you the way they looked at the dust on the court floor. You have survived the road and the machine at its end. Whether the wall was worth it is a question for people who can breathe here.
outcomes.failure:
You put both hands into the seam and push, and the drive answers with the full force the plate promised. The leaves reverse. The gap that had been widening comes back with your arms in it, then your shoulder, and the scored edge that caught someone before catches you.

You are pinned, half through, when the Warden's cannon finishes coming back to speed. It fires through the narrowing seam. The burst takes what the gate has not, and the last thing the clean air does is reach you, once, one breath of rain and filtered metal, before the leaves finish closing and lock with your body between them, within sight of everything you walked here for.
outcomes.critical_success:
You feel it before you see it: the failing gear hesitates on a tooth that is already half gone, and you put your whole weight against the leaf in exactly that instant. The gear does not slip. It shears. The drive, freed of it, runs out to its stop with a shriek, and the gate opens the full width of the passage and stays there, its lock hunting for a leaf that is no longer where it expects.

You walk through standing up. Clean air comes past you both ways, out into the court and in with you, and the plate's promise of a crushing closure now belongs to nobody, because the gate has nothing left to close with. Behind the glass the guard is talking into a radio, fast. For once the thing you did to survive has left a door open behind you that someone else could use, and you do not stop to see who.
outcomes.critical_failure:
The weakened gear does not fight you. It lets go all at once, and the leaf you were pushing against is suddenly not there, and your own weight carries you forward through the gap and under the frame as the drive, with nothing holding it, drops.

The descending frame is the thing the plate meant. It comes down on you from above with the full mass of the gate behind it, and there is no time in it for a decision, only the sound of the seam closing and clean air on your face for as long as a single breath, rain and filtered metal, before steel and the floor meet through you. The lock engages. The gate records nothing. It was closing anyway.

outcomes.success:
The controller is the same make as the relays that lit the powered run under the rail line for you, the ones somebody had been cleaning: the same interval in its clicks, the same order to its lamps. You learned that interval walking it. You give the panel the emergency sequence in that rhythm, command, pause, command, and the red border around the diagram goes out.

The controller accepts one final instruction and spends what power it has left on the drive. The gate opens the width of a body and no more, and you go through it with your shoulders turned, and it grinds shut behind you and locks. Beyond it a corridor runs away under white light, clean and unexplained, with no one in it yet. The relay lamps you followed east were leading somewhere after all. They were leading here, and here has not decided what you are.
outcomes.failure:
You run the emergency sequence and the controller recognizes it as unauthorized on the third command. It does exactly what the red border said it would. The frame energizes, all of it, and the current takes you across the palm and up the arm and through the chest before the hand can be told to let go, because hands do not let go of that; they close.

You are aware of the smell first and of the glove fused beside yours second, and then of nothing in particular. The gate stays a hand's width open. The controller records a rejected entry, the way it recorded the last one, and the clean air goes on coming through the gap to a floor where nobody is breathing it.
outcomes.critical_success:
You have read one of these before. The controller is a smaller cousin of the Citadel hardware you read under the rail line, and once you see that, its diagram stops being a warning and becomes a map. You run the emergency sequence clean, first time, every command in its interval, and the controller does more than accept: it restores the full gate cycle.

The leaves draw back the entire width of the passage on a drive that suddenly sounds healthy, and a row of green lamps comes on along the floor of the corridor beyond, leading in. You walk through upright, not sideways, with clean air coming at you down the whole length of the corridor. Behind the glass the guard has gone very still. The gate has been told, by its own controller, that you are authorized, and nobody has said yet who told the controller.
outcomes.critical_failure:
The first command bridges two circuits the diagram kept apart with a red line, and there is no third command. Full gate voltage crosses the panel and crosses you with it. Your heart stops before your hand can withdraw, and your hand does not withdraw either; it stays on the frame beside the fused glove of the last person who did this, and the Citadel now has two.

The controller resets. The gate stays a hand's width open above a body it will file as an electrical fault, and the guard behind the glass looks away first. Clean air comes through the gap and finds nobody. It was the last door, and it was armed, and the diagram said so.

outcomes.success:
You look up at the glass and speak to the guard, not to the gate. You tell them the machine that made this decision for them is on its side on their own court, and the next decision is theirs, as a person, before some other procedure arrives to make it. Every mile behind you is in your voice, and you let it be. You do not ask. You tell them to open it now.

The rifle above the glass does not fire. For a long moment nothing does. Then a hand you have not seen before reaches across the guard's console to the override, a human hand, hesitating over the switch as if it were hot, and throws it. The drive picks up. The gate opens just enough for a body and you go through it before anyone up there can change their mind, and it locks behind you, and on the other side a person, not a recording, says something you do not catch.
outcomes.failure:
You tell the guard to open it now, and the guard steps back from the glass. It is not refusal, not yet; it is a person getting out of the way of a decision, and the decision has a standing order behind it that the machine's death did not cancel.

The barrel in the open aperture above the glass comes down a few degrees. You see it happen, and there is nowhere on the court to be that it cannot see. The first round takes you in the chest and the second is unnecessary, and you go down with your back against the gate that is still open a hand's width behind you, clean air coming through the gap onto the back of your neck. The guard has not moved from where they stepped to. The lights above were meant for someone, and it was not the person on the floor.
outcomes.critical_success:
The badge on the guard's chest has a name on it, and you read it through the glass and say it. Not the gate's name for them, theirs. You tell them, by name, that the Warden is on the floor, that the machine that used to decide this is finished, and that the person left in the room is going to decide it now.

The name does what argument could not. They are already moving before you finish, one hand on the override, and the gate opens wider than a body and stays. Then they say your name back to you, off the screening record on their console, which has your name on it whether or not you ever gave it, and reach through and pull you in by the coat before anyone else up there can find a reason not to. The gate locks behind you. Somebody in the Citadel knows your name, and chose.
outcomes.critical_failure:
Your demand becomes noise inside the armored glass; you can see it become noise, the guard's face closing on it. They do not look at the override. They look up, at the aperture over their own head, and give the smallest nod anyone has ever given, and the rifle resting in it fires the volley the standing order asks for.

It erases every word before the gate can answer any of them. You are on the court beside the Warden you broke, and it is still talking, the recording going on about contamination to a floor with two bodies on it now, one steel and one not. The clean air keeps coming through the hand's width of gap. Behind the glass, the guard sits down. The decision was theirs, as a person, and they made it.
